# SPARK regulates AGC kinases central to the Toxoplasma gondii asexual cycle ## Authors - Alice L Herneisen1 ([ORCID: 0000-0003-3368-0893](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3368-0893)) - Michelle L Peters1 - Tyler A Smith1 - Emily Shortt1 - Sebastian Lourido1 ([ORCID: 0000-0002-5237-1095](https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5237-1095)) † ### Affiliations 1. Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research and Department of Biology, Massachusetts Institute of Technology Cambridge United States ([ROR:042nb2s44](https://ror.org/042nb2s44)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract Apicomplexan parasites balance proliferation, persistence, and spread in their metazoan hosts. AGC kinases, such as PKG, PKA, and the PDK1 ortholog SPARK, integrate environmental signals to toggle parasites between replicative and motile life stages. Recent studies have cataloged pathways downstream of apicomplexan PKG and PKA; however, less is known about the global integration of AGC kinase signaling cascades. Here, conditional genetics coupled to unbiased proteomics demonstrates that SPARK complexes with an elongin-like protein to regulate the stability of PKA and PKG in the model apicomplexan Toxoplasma gondii. Defects attributed to SPARK depletion develop after PKG and PKA are down-regulated. Parasites lacking SPARK differentiate into the chronic form of infection, which may arise from reduced activity of a coccidian-specific PKA ortholog. This work delineates the signaling topology of AGC kinases that together control transitions within the asexual cycle of this important family of parasites. ## Introduction Apicomplexans parasitize a majority of warm-blooded species, including an estimated quarter of the human population (Jones et al., 2014). Central to parasite success is the ability to transition between different life cycle stages to balance proliferation and transmission (Lourido, 2019). The acute phase of infection by Toxoplasma gondii, a model apicomplexan, induces the pathology of disease. Parasites invade host cells, establish an intracellular niche that subverts innate immune responses, replicate, and exit the host via lysis to establish new sites of infection (Blader et al., 2015). These pathogens adapt to the inverted ion and nutrient gradients within and without the host cell in minutes. Such rapid changes in cellular state depend on signal transduction in T. gondii and related apicomplexans. Second messenger cascades within the parasite cytoplasm are especially well-suited to rapidly transduce and amplify signals from a changing environment. Accordingly, apicomplexans—and T. gondii in particular—have a complete repertoire of second messenger signaling components, from kinases to cyclases and phosphodiesterases (Brown et al., 2020; Pace et al., 2020). The roles of second messenger kinases—collectively referred to as AGC kinases for the founding members protein kinases A, G, and C—in apicomplexan life cycles have been elaborated in candidate-by-candidate approaches. cGMP-dependent protein kinase (or protein kinase G, PKG) is necessary for the secretion of parasite-specific adhesins and perforins, enabling efficient escape and invasion of host cells (Brown et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2016; Wiersma et al., 2004). In apicomplexan cells, PKG operates upstream of calcium release and thus potentiates an orthogonal second messenger signaling network. Consequently, PKG inhibitors have been pursued as anti-parasitic compounds (Baker et al., 2017; Donald et al., 2006; Sidik et al., 2016a). Another cyclic-nucleotide-dependent protein kinase, PKA, similarly promotes parasite spread during infection; in Plasmodium spp. merozoites, PKA function enables parasite invasion of host cells (Flueck et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2019; Wilde et al., 2019), and in T. gondii balanced PKA C1 function is required to ensure that parasites do not exit the host cell prematurely (Jia et al., 2017; Uboldi et al., 2018). T. gondii has an additional ortholog of the PKA catalytic subunit, PKA C3, which maintains parasites in the acute phase of the infection and reduces conversion to a slowly proliferating, chronic infection termed the bradyzoite stage (Sugi et al., 2016). Several recent studies have sought to characterize the downstream targets of second messenger kinases in apicomplexans, including PKA, PKG, and calcium-dependent protein kinases (Alam et al., 2015; Balestra et al., 2021; Brochet et al., 2014; Chan et al., 2023; Herneisen et al., 2022; Jia et al., 2017; Nofal et al., 2022). The second messenger networks in these parasites are intricately interwoven, with documented crosstalk between parasite cAMP, cGMP, and calcium signaling cascades. Comparatively little work has addressed upstream signal integration in apicomplexans. In metazoans, growth factor kinases such as mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) and phosphoinositide-dependent protein kinase 1 (PDK1) prime numerous AGC kinases for further second messenger-based activation (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012; Mora et al., 2004). We recently identified the Store Potentiating/Activating Regulatory Kinase (SPARK), an apicomplexan ortholog of metazoan PDK1, as a fitness-conferring candidate in pooled screens of the T. gondii kinome. Parasites depleted of SPARK for multiple replication cycles failed to enter and exit host cells upon stimulation with zaprinast, a chemical that elevates cGMP in parasites (Smith et al., 2022). The Plasmodium falciparum ortholog of SPARK has been implicated in invasion and proliferation through the regulation of the PKA pathway (Hitz et al., 2021). Although parasites with disrupted SPARK alleles were characterized phenotypically, evidence for the PDK1 activity of SPARK was indirect. Here, we map the topology of the signaling network regulated by SPARK in T. gondii. SPARK complexes with an elongin-like protein we name SPARKEL. Phenotypic and proteomic experiments show that SPARK dysregulation lessens PKA C1, PKG, and PKA C3 function. Phenotypes attributed to SPARK depletion—reduced invasion, host cell lysis, calcium signaling, and increased differentiation—can be explained by the attenuated activities of SPARK’s client kinases. The proper functioning of SPARK thus ensures that T. gondii progresses through the acute stage of its infection cycle. ## Results ### SPARK complexes with an elongin-like protein, SPARKEL To identify proteins interacting with SPARK, we immunopurified the mNG epitope of the previously described SPARK-mNG-AID strain (Smith et al., 2022) with anti-mNG nanobodies and quantified protein abundance using label-free quantitative proteomics (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1). The immunoprecipitation (IP) successfully enriched SPARK as well as a hypothetical protein, TGGT1_291010. IPs with lysates of parasites expressing SPARK-mNG lacking AID demonstrated that the interaction was not due to the presence of the degron; TGGT1_291010 was once again highly enriched (Figure 1A), along with a putative AGC kinase (TGGT1_205550). The AGC kinase is restricted to coccidians but is dispensable during acute T. gondii infection (Sidik et al., 2016b); we therefore focused our efforts on the hypothetical protein, which contributes to parasite fitness. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/93877/elife-93877-fig1-v1.jpg) **Figure 1.:** (A) Protein abundances from immunopurified SPARK-mNG lysates or an untagged control strain. TGGT1_291010 is a 23 kDa protein with a C-terminal SKP1/BTB/POZ domain (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). This domain shares homology with that seen in metazoan Elongin C. For this reason, we named the gene TGGT1_291010 ‘SPARK Elongin-Like protein’ (SPARKEL, Table 1). SPARKEL homologs are found in the free-living alveolates Vitrella brassicaformis and Chromera velia but are absent in Aconoidasida (Figure 1C), suggesting that the gene was present in the ancestor of apicomplexans but was selectively lost in some lineages. The function of proteins with Elongin C-like domains has not been widely investigated in unicellular eukaryotes. **Table 1.** Proteins discussed in the text.

Immunoprecipitation and mass spectrometry of SPARKEL enriched SPARK (Figure 1D and Supplementary file 1) and several putative components of daughter cell replication, including TGGT1_212770 (Dos Santos Pacheco et al., 2021), BCC10, and EFPP/BCC5. To confirm that SPARKEL and SPARK interact in situ, we introduced a C-terminal TurboID fusion at the SPARKEL endogenous locus (Branon et al., 2018). These transgenic parasites were treated with biotin while intracellular, and biotinylated proteins were enriched from lysates via streptavidin affinity purification. As a control, we conducted a parallel experiment with transgenic parasites expressing TurboID fused to a cytosolic mNG fluorophore. SPARK and the AGC kinase TGGT1_205550 were highly enriched in the SPARKEL proximity labeling experiment (Figure 1E and Supplementary file 2). A proximity labeling experiment with parasites expressing TurboID at the N terminus of SPARKEL similarly enriched SPARK and TGGT1_205550 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 2). Thus, the interactions between SPARK, SPARKEL, and TGGT1_205550 were consistently observed across a variety of approaches. Endogenous tagging of SPARK and SPARKEL in the same parasite strain revealed punctate cytosolic staining for each protein (Figure 1F); however, the low expression level of SPARKEL precluded robust colocalization. Nevertheless, strong mass spectrometry evidence for the physical interaction between SPARK and SPARKEL motivated further analysis of their functional relationship. ### SPARK and SPARKEL depletion phenocopy at multiple steps in the lytic cycle To determine the regulatory interaction between SPARK and SPARKEL, we first generated a SPARKEL conditional knockdown allele by inserting V5, HaloTag, mini auxin-inducible degron (mAID), and Ty epitopes at the endogenous SPARKEL C terminus. In this strain, we tagged SPARK with a C-terminal V5-mCherry-HA. Parasites treated with auxin (indole-3-acetic acid; IAA) to deplete SPARKEL failed to form plaques in host cell monolayers (Figure 2A). As indicated by immunoblot, IAA treatment led to a reduction in detectable SPARKEL signal within 1 hr, as well as co-depletion of SPARK on a similar time scale (Figure 2B). We next generated a strain expressing SPARK-V5-mAID-HA. Similarly, SPARK levels were reduced within 1 hr of IAA addition (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), as reported for a similar strain previously (Smith et al., 2022). In this genetic background, we tagged SPARKEL endogenously with a C-terminal V5-mNG-Ty. IAA treatment reduced SPARK levels and led to a reduction in SPARKEL abundance (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Despite the low abundance of SPARK and SPARKEL, individual phosphopeptides were detected for each protein. To uncover the molecular pathways regulated by SPARK, we performed enrichment analysis of the phosphopeptides exhibiting the highest degree of altered abundance upon SPARK depletion (Figure 3G). Changes in SPARK function likely alter post-translational modification (PTM) cascades both directly and indirectly. SPARK depletion reduced the abundance of phosphopeptides belonging to cyclic nucleotide-regulated kinases, which was in part driven by a reduction in kinase abundance. SPARK depletion also coincided with a reduction in phosphosites on several phosphatases (Table 1), including BCC6, PPM1, and an uncharacterized dual-specificity phosphatase. These kinases are united by general structural features required for activity and integrity, such as the activation segment (also known as the activation loop or T-loop), and the C-terminal hydrophobic and turn motifs, which are common loci of regulation that can position the kinase into an active conformation. In mammals, AGC kinases depend on PDK1 in various ways. For example, phosphorylation of the Akt (PKB) activation loop by PDK1 leads to partial activation; additional phosphorylation by the target of rapamycin (mTOR) complex produces maximal activity (Pearce et al., 2010). Some protein kinase C (PKC) isoforms undergo sequential phosphorylation by upstream enzymes—including PDK1—that prime PKC for activity and prevent kinase degradation (Newton, 2010). PKA catalytic isoforms require T-loop phosphorylation for activity; however, whether this modification is installed autocatalytically or by PDK1 depends on the cellular context (Cheng et al., 1998; Moore et al., 2002; Williams et al., 2000). Consequently, PDK1 dysregulation provokes diverse cellular consequences, including enhanced growth, migration, and cell survival—processes associated with cancer in animals (Gagliardi et al., 2018; Mora et al., 2004; Raimondi and Falasca, 2011). In this study, we characterize the diverse consequences of the PDK1 ortholog dysregulation in the ubiquitous and divergent eukaryotic parasite of animals, T. gondii. A prior study identified SPARK as a regulator of parasite invasion and egress following 24 hr of kinase depletion (Smith et al., 2022). Unexpectedly, we observed that three h of SPARK depletion were insufficient to impact T. gondii motility or calcium-dependent signaling, indicating that the phenotypes associated with SPARK depletion develop over time. A similar time delay was observed for the development of phenotypes following depletion of the SPARK-interacting protein SPARKEL. Quantitative proteomics revealed that PKA and PKG abundances began to decrease after more than 3 hr of SPARK depletion. Proximity labeling experiments also suggested that SPARK, PKA, and PKG are spatially associated within the parasite cell. We propose a model in which SPARK is required for the activation and stabilization of PKG and PKA. From our own studies, multiple mass spectrometric and cell biological experiments support the relationship between SPARK and AGC kinases. Furthermore, PDK1 mutations in the related apicomplexan Plasmodium falciparum were observed to suppress toxicity related to overexpression of PfPKA (Hitz et al., 2021). Both TgPKG and TgPKA C1 possess features of AGC kinases involved in PDK1 interaction, such as the PDK1-interacting fragment FXXF. PKA C1 terminates in the sequence FTSW, whereas PKG has two non-terminal FXXF motifs, FGDF and FLYF. Although these motifs are not strictly C-terminal, as in animals, their position resembles that observed in some plant AGC kinases, up to 50 amino acids upstream of the C terminus (Rademacher and Offringa, 2012). The T-loop phosphorylation sites of each kinase—PKA C1 T190 and PKG T838—were detected in the global phosphoproteome and were down-regulated following SPARK knockdown. The requirement of T-loop threonine phosphorylation for PKG activity is unclear, as recombinant Plasmodium spp. PKG was still active when this residue was mutated (El Bakkouri et al., 2019). Conformational changes due to cGMP binding—in particular, rearrangement of the N-terminal autoinhibitory segment otherwise adjacent to the activation loop—appeared particularly important for PKG activity. Upon SPARK depletion, multiple phosphorylation sites in the N-terminal and cyclic nucleotide–binding domains of PKG (T16, S20, S22, T59, S62, T96, T99, and S129) decrease in abundance, whereas others remain stable or increase (S40 and S105). Thus, phosphorylation may function in the regulation of these domains. Heterologous expression and activity assays of PKA C1 and PKG may resolve the importance of activation loop and cyclic nucleotide–domain phosphorylation for kinase function; however, such biochemical assays are not currently available for the T. gondii kinases. The cause for reduction of PKA C1 and PKG levels also requires further study; in principle, active degradation or dilution mechanisms due to new protein synthesis and cell division are possible. In support of the latter, down-regulation of both kinases was only observed after 8 hr of SPARK depletion, a period longer than the T. gondii cell cycle. SPARK could also indirectly stabilize PKA C1 and PKG abundances, for example by phosphorylating and inhibiting a ubiquitin ligase. One candidate could be the HECT domain protein TGGT1_280660, which exhibited SPARK-dependent phosphoregulation and was enriched in SPARK proximity labeling experiments. Examination of the SPARK-dependent ubiquitinome or pulse-chase phosphoproteomics experiments could yield further insight into the mechanisms of PKA C1 and PKG down-regulation following SPARK depletion. Independent of biochemical mechanisms, genetic evidence supports the hypothesis that SPARK phenotypes associated with kinetic transitions in the lytic cycle—such as motility, egress, and invasion—arise from dysregulated PKA C1 and PKG activities. In T. gondii, PKA negatively regulates egress and positively regulates the transition between invasion and the establishment of a replicative niche (Jia et al., 2017; Uboldi et al., 2018); by contrast, in P. falciparum, PKA mediates parasite invasion (Flueck et al., 2019; Patel et al., 2019; Wilde et al., 2019). PKG is more broadly required for apicomplexan motility, invasion, and egress and functions by mobilizing parasite intracellular calcium stores. Genetic pathway analysis of T. gondii PKA C1 and PKG inhibition supports a model in which PKG lies downstream of PKA (Jia et al., 2017). Increasingly, proteomic, genetic, and physiological studies implicate negative feedback mechanisms between cAMP and cGMP signaling pathways in apicomplexans (Alam et al., 2015; Bisio et al., 2019; Brochet et al., 2014; Moss et al., 2022; Nofal et al., 2022). In T. gondii, SPARK inhibition releases the brakes that PKA C1 holds on egress and jams the engine of PKG activity, resulting in parasite stasis. The PKA signaling circuit differs in Plasmodium spp., where a sole PKA C subunit is indispensable for invasion but not egress (Patel et al., 2019; Wilde et al., 2019). However, SPARK inhibition would lead to a similarly inhibitory effect on parasite proliferation, as has been suggested recently in studies employing altered P. falciparum PDK1 and PKA alleles (Hitz et al., 2021). T. gondii has two additional paralogs of the PKA catalytic subunit, relative to Plasmodium spp., PKA C2 and PKA C3. PKA C2 expression levels are low outside of the parasite sexual stages (Ramakrishnan et al., 2019; Sugi et al., 2016). PKA C3 disruption was previously reported to increase conversion to the bradyzoite stage (Sugi et al., 2016). Our results using a PKA C3 conditional knockdown support this finding. Furthermore, PKA C3 and SPARK associate, as revealed through approaches that probe reciprocal interactions. PKA C3 possesses a canonical PDK1-interacting fragment (FDNF) and shares an activation loop motif with PKA C1. Although PKA C3 peptide levels were below the detection limit in our depletion phosphoproteome experiments, we propose that SPARK depletion leads to down-regulation of PKA C3 activity separately from a reduction in PKA C3 protein abundance. SPARK and PKA C3 depletion phenocopy each other with respect to in vitro differentiation. Candidates for the molecular targets responsible for differentiation may reside in the overlapping phosphosites in the SPARK and PKA C3 depletion phosphoproteomes. The regulation of SPARK remains an open inquiry. Mammalian PDK1 is constitutively active due to auto-phosphorylation in trans. The PH domain triggers mammalian PDK1 homodimerization upon binding of phosphatidylinositol (3,4,5)-trisphosphate (Levina et al., 2022; Masters et al., 2010; Pearce et al., 2010). SPARK lacks the PH domain Smith et al., 2022; therefore, apicomplexans have likely evolved alternative mechanisms for regulating PDK1. The complex of proteins interacting with SPARK—the elongin-like protein SPARKEL and the putative AGC kinase TGME49_205550—may represent a means of modulating SPARK activity. Elongin C forms a component of multiprotein complexes. E3 ubiquitin ligases are well-known examples; however, elongin C can affect steady-state protein levels through mechanisms distinct from ubiquitination (Hyman et al., 2002). In metazoans, PDK1 has been reported to associate with E3 ligases and exhibit monobiquitination (Jiang et al., 2021; Uras et al., 2012). However, the SPARK and SPARKEL IPs and proximity experiments failed to identify obvious components of stable ubiquitin ligase complexes. Given the co-depletion of the complex—as has been reported for other tightly associated proteins studied with the AID system (Tosetti et al., 2020)—further biochemical studies are required to discern the regulatory interactions between SPARK and SPARKEL. Unlike most apicomplexans, Plasmodium spp. appear to have lost SPARKEL, possibly requiring alternative mechanisms to control SPARK activity. Our unbiased and integrative proteomic approaches uncovered ancient features of signaling networks de novo and revealed how such relationships can be repurposed for parasitism. Apicomplexans are well-adapted to transition between life stages in their hosts. Synthesizing genetic, proteomic, and phenotypic data, we propose that SPARK fundamentally integrates cyclic nucleotide signaling networks in apicomplexan parasites. In T. gondii, proper SPARK function preserves tachyzoite physiology by activating PKG, PKA C1, and PKA C3, thus promoting cycling within the acute stages of the infection over differentiation into the chronic stage wherein AGC kinase activity is lower (Fu et al., 2021). In principle, SPARK may serve as a central node for regulation of the asexual stages. ## Materials and methods ### Reagents and cell culture T. gondii parasites of the type I RH strain ∆ku80/∆hxgprt genetic background ATCC PRA-319, (Huynh and Carruthers, 2009) or the type II ME49 strain ∆ku80/∆hxgprt background (Waldman et al., 2020) were grown in human foreskin fibroblasts (HFFs, ATCC SCRC-1041; male) maintained in DMEM (GIBCO) supplemented with 3% calf serum and 10 μg/mL gentamicin (Thermo Fisher Scientific). ## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.93877.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.93877.3.sa1)

Summary:

Herneisen et al characterise the Toxoplasma PDK1 orthologue SPARK and an associated protein SPARKEL (cute name) in controlling important fate decisions in Toxoplasma. Over recent years this group and others have characterised the role of cAMP and cGMP signalling in negatively and positively regulating egress, motility and invasion, respectively. This manuscript furthers this work by showing that SPARK and SPARKEL likely act upstream, or at least control the levels of the cAMP and cGMP-dependent kinases PKA and PKG, respectively, thus controlling the transition of intracellular replicating parasites into extracellular motile forms (and back again).

The authors use quantitative (phospho)proteomic techniques to elegantly demonstrate the upstream role of SPARK in controlling cAMP and cGMP pathways. They use sophisticated analysis techniques (at least for parasitology) to show the functional association between cGMP and cAMP signalling pathways. They therefore begin to unify our understanding of the complicated signalling pathways used by Toxoplasma to control key regulatory processes that control the activation and suppression of motility. The authors then use molecular and cellular assays on a range of generated transgenic lines to back up their observations made by quantitative proteomics that are clear in their design and approach.

The authors then extend their work by showing that SPARK/SPARKEL also control PKAc3 function. PKAc3 has previously been shown to negatively regulate differentiation into bradyzoite forms and this work backs up and extends this finding to show that SPARK also controls this. The authors conclude that SPARK could act as a central node of regulation of the asexual stage, keeping parasites in their lytic cell growth and preventing differentiation. Whether this is true is beyond the scope of this paper and will have to be determined at a later date.

Strengths:

This is an exceptional body of work. It is elegantly performed, with state-of-the-art proteomic methodologies carefully being applied to Toxoplasma. Observations from the proteomic datasets are masterfully backed up with validation using quantitative molecular and cellular biology assays.

The paper is carefully and concisely written and is not overreaching in its conclusions. This work and its analysis set a new benchmark for the use of proteomics and molecular genetics in apicomplexan parasites.

Weaknesses:

There are no weaknesses in this paper.

Summary:

The manuscript by Herneisen et al. examines the Toxoplasma SPARK kinase orthologous to mammalian PDK1 kinase. The extracellular signals trigger cascades of the second messengers and play a central role in the apicomplexan parasites' survival. In Toxoplasma, these cascades regulate active replication of the tachyzoites, which manifests as acute toxoplasmosis, or the development into drug-resilient bradyzoites characteristic of the chronic stage of the disease. This study focuses on the poorly understood signaling mechanisms acting upstream of such second messenger kinases as PKA and PKG. The authors showed that similar to PDK1, Toxoplasma SPARK likely regulates several AGC kinases.

Weaknesses:

Although the revised manuscript has significantly improved, the primary concern of incomplete data analysis still needs to be addressed.

results.result: SPARK physically interacts with an elongin-like protein named SPARKEL (TGGT1_291010). This interaction was demonstrated through multiple orthogonal approaches including immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry (IP-MS) and proximity labeling (TurboID) experiments, which consistently enriched SPARKEL in SPARK pulldowns and vice versa. SPARKEL is a 23 kDa protein containing a C-terminal SKP1/BTB/POZ domain with homology to metazoan Elongin C.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C24-C27, C32-C33, C38, C41-C44 collectively demonstrate the SPARK-SPARKEL interaction through multiple independent experimental approaches (IP-MS with and without degron, reciprocal IP, TurboID from both N- and C-termini). The consistency across methods and the structural characterization of SPARKEL provide strong converging evidence for this protein-protein interaction.

results.result: SPARKEL homologs are present in free-living alveolates (Vitrella brassicaformis and Chromera velia) but absent in Aconoidasida, suggesting the gene was present in the apicomplexan ancestor but selectively lost in some lineages.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C36 describe phylogenetic distribution based on sequence analysis and are supported by Figure 1C showing the phylogenetic tree. The inference about ancestral presence and selective loss (C36) is reasonable given the phylogenetic pattern, though alternative evolutionary scenarios (e.g., horizontal gene transfer) are not explicitly ruled out.

results.result: Conditional depletion of SPARKEL via the auxin-inducible degron (AID) system leads to co-depletion of SPARK within 1 hour, and vice versa. Parasites depleted of SPARKEL fail to form plaques in host cell monolayers. However, both proteins have low abundance approaching the limit of detection.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C51 demonstrate reciprocal co-depletion through immunoblot experiments (Figure 2B-C) and functional consequences (plaque assays, Figure 2A). The co-depletion is well-documented, though C52 appropriately notes the technical limitation of low protein abundance. The authors acknowledge they cannot formally exclude degradation products running at expected molecular weights.

results.result: SPARK and SPARKEL depletion phenotypes develop over time. After 24 hours of IAA treatment, parasites show reduced invasion, egress efficiency, and calcium mobilization. However, 3 hours of depletion is insufficient to impact motility or calcium signaling, indicating phenotypes develop gradually rather than acutely.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C60 describe time-course phenotypic characterization with appropriate controls. The distinction between 3-hour and 24-hour timepoints is well-supported by multiple assays (replication, invasion, egress, calcium imaging; Figure 2D-J). The conclusion that phenotypes develop over time (C57, C60) is justified by the data, though the molecular mechanism remains unclear.

results.result: Extended SPARK or SPARKEL depletion (24 hours) leads to down-regulation of PKG and PKA catalytic and regulatory subunits, with protein abundances beginning to drop after 8 hours of IAA treatment. Concurrently, bradyzoite-specific proteins (MAG1, BRP1, CST1, CST10, MIC13, BFD2) are up-regulated, primarily between 8-24 hours of treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C68 are supported by quantitative proteomics with TMT multiplexing and time-course analysis (Figure 3A, C-D, Table 1). The temporal dynamics are well-characterized with appropriate biological replicates. The conclusion that SPARK-SPARKEL depletion affects both AGC kinase stability and stage-specific protein expression is well-supported.

results.result: Phosphoproteomics of SPARK depletion identified 18,518 phosphopeptides, revealing broad effects on post-translational modification cascades. SPARK depletion reduced phosphorylation of cyclic nucleotide-regulated kinases and several phosphatases, while increasing phosphorylation of other kinases and phosphatases. Down-regulated phosphosites include proteins involved in DNA accessibility, transcription, RNA modification, and transport. Gaussian mixture modeling clustered phosphopeptides into seven kinetically distinct response signatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C79 describe comprehensive phosphoproteomics analysis with appropriate statistical methods (PCA, modified Z-scores, Gaussian mixture modeling). The scale of the dataset (18,518 phosphopeptides) and clustering analysis (Figure 3H) support the conclusion of broad cellular effects. Gene ontology enrichment (Figure 3G) validates functional categories, though some effects may be indirect.

results.result: SPARK proximity labeling (TurboID) identified PKG as enriched and PKA C1 as narrowly missing cutoffs. A putative HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase (TGGT1_280660) with SPARK-dependent phosphoregulation was also identified. PKA C3, a coccidian-specific PKA ortholog, was enriched in the SPARK-TurboID experiment.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C83 describe TurboID proximity labeling results (Figure 3I, Supplementary file 3). The enrichment of PKG and PKA C3 is well-supported, though PKA C1 narrowly missing cutoffs (C81) suggests borderline significance. The integration with phosphoproteomics data (C82) strengthens the evidence for functional relationships.

results.result: SPARK depletion reduces phosphorylation of PKA C1 activation loop (T190) and C-terminal tail (T341), as well as PKA R N-terminal phosphosites (S17, S27, S94). PKA C1 and PKA R protein levels decrease after 8 hours of SPARK depletion, as confirmed by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry, without changes in transcript levels. PKA C1-dependent phosphopeptides significantly decrease between 8-24 hours of SPARK depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C91 integrate phosphoproteomics (Figure 4A-B), qRT-PCR (Figure 4—supplement 1), immunofluorescence (Figure 4D), and flow cytometry (Figure 4E-F) to demonstrate post-translational regulation of PKA C1/R. The lack of transcript changes (C87) supports protein-level regulation. Comparative analysis with PKA R depletion phosphoproteome (Figure 4G) strengthens the conclusion about PKA C1 substrate regulation.

results.result: SPARK depletion reduces phosphorylation of PKG N-terminal sites and activation loop (T838). SPARK-depleted parasites are sensitized to PKG inhibitor Compound 1 in A23187-induced egress assays, suggesting decreased PKG activity. PKG-dependent phosphopeptides significantly decrease between 8-24 hours of SPARK depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 combine phosphoproteomics (Figure 5A) with chemical-genetic validation (Figure 5B-C) and comparative analysis with PKG depletion phosphoproteome (Figure 5D). The sensitization to Compound 1 (C93) provides functional evidence for reduced PKG activity, though the mechanism (reduced protein vs. reduced activity) requires further investigation.

results.result: Prolonged SPARK, SPARKEL, or PKA C3 depletion elevates differentiation to bradyzoites under normal and alkaline stress conditions, as measured by dolichos lectin staining. PKA C3 depletion phenocopies SPARK/SPARKEL depletion. Differentiation depends on the BFD1 transcriptional circuit, as SPARK-AID/Δbfd1 and PKA C3-AID/Δbfd1 mutants fail to differentiate. PKG or CDPK1 depletion does not enhance differentiation, indicating egress defects alone are insufficient.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C106 demonstrate stage conversion through multiple approaches: immunofluorescence (Figure 6A-H), genetic epistasis with BFD1 knockout (Figure 6G-H), and transcriptomics (Figure 6I). The specificity is supported by negative controls (PKG, CDPK1 depletion; C101) and validation in ME49 strain (C102). The BFD1-dependence (C103-C104) is well-supported, though the molecular mechanism linking SPARK/PKA C3 to BFD1 activation remains unclear.

results.result: PKA C3 physically interacts with SPARK, as demonstrated by reciprocal immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry. SPARKEL was also co-purified with PKA C3 to a lesser extent. PKA C3 does not interact with the canonical PKA regulatory subunit, consistent with prior reports. Together with TurboID data, these results support a strong physical interaction between SPARK and PKA C3.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C110 demonstrate SPARK-PKA C3 interaction through IP-MS (Figure 7A) and integrate with TurboID data (Figure 3I). The consistency with prior literature (C109) and reciprocal validation strengthen the conclusion. However, the stoichiometry and functional significance of the interaction require further investigation.

results.result: Unlike PKA C1, PKA C3 protein levels are not reduced following SPARK depletion. After 24 hours of IAA treatment, PKA C3 levels are unaltered or slightly elevated by immunoblot, with a non-significant trend toward increased abundance by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C113 are supported by immunoblot (Figure 7B-C), immunofluorescence, and flow cytometry (Figure 7D-F). The distinction from PKA C1 regulation is important for the model. However, the trend toward increased PKA C3 (C112) is not statistically significant, and the biological significance is unclear.

results.result: PKA C3 depletion phosphoproteomics identified 4,792 proteins and 12,721 phosphopeptides, with up-regulation of bradyzoite-stage proteins. Gaussian mixture modeling clustered phosphopeptides into three classes. PKA C3-dependent phosphopeptides significantly decrease within 3 hours of SPARK depletion, faster than the bulk phosphoproteome. However, SPARK and PKA C3 phosphoproteomes diverge regarding dense granule protein regulation, with some PKA C3-dependent phosphopeptides increasing upon SPARK depletion.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C120 describe PKA C3 depletion phosphoproteomics with appropriate statistical analysis (PCA, clustering, comparative analysis; Figure 7H-K). The rapid decrease of PKA C3-dependent phosphopeptides upon SPARK depletion (C118) supports functional regulation. The divergence in dense granule protein regulation (C119) is interesting but mechanistically unclear, possibly reflecting indirect effects or compensation by other kinases.

results.result: The authors propose a model in which SPARK is required for activation and stabilization of PKG, PKA C1, and PKA C3. Genetic evidence supports that SPARK phenotypes (motility, egress, invasion) arise from dysregulated PKA C1 and PKG activities. In T. gondii, SPARK inhibition releases PKA C1 brakes on egress while reducing PKG activity, resulting in parasite stasis. Proper SPARK function preserves tachyzoite physiology and promotes acute-stage cycling over differentiation to bradyzoites.
results.evaluation: Claims C132, C145, C151, C179-C180 present the central model integrating genetic, proteomic, and phenotypic data. The model is well-supported by: (1) physical interactions (IP-MS, TurboID), (2) temporal correlation between kinase down-regulation and phenotype development, (3) phosphoproteomics showing reduced kinase activity signatures, (4) chemical-genetic validation (Compound 1 sensitization), and (5) epistasis experiments (BFD1 dependence). However, direct biochemical evidence for SPARK kinase activity on PKA/PKG is lacking.

results.result: Quantitative proteomics revealed PKA and PKG abundances begin to decrease after more than 3 hours of SPARK depletion. Proximity labeling experiments suggest SPARK, PKA, and PKG are spatially associated within the parasite cell.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C131 summarize key findings from time-course proteomics and TurboID experiments. The temporal dynamics (C130) are well-supported by Figure 3C. Spatial association (C131) is inferred from TurboID enrichment, though the resolution of proximity labeling (~10 nm radius) does not prove direct interaction.

results.result: TgPKG and TgPKA C1 possess PDK1-interacting fragment (FXXF) motifs: PKA C1 terminates in FTSW, while PKG has two non-terminal FXXF motifs (FGDF and FLYF). PKA C3 possesses a canonical PDK1-interacting fragment (FDNF) and shares an activation loop motif with PKA C1. T-loop phosphorylation sites (PKA C1 T190, PKG T838) were detected and down-regulated following SPARK knockdown.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C137, C158-C159 describe sequence features and phosphorylation sites. The presence of FXXF motifs is supported by sequence analysis, and T-loop phosphorylation changes are documented in phosphoproteomics (Figure 4A, 5A). However, the functional importance of these motifs for SPARK interaction is not directly tested (e.g., through mutagenesis).

results.result: The requirement of T-loop threonine phosphorylation for PKG activity is unclear, as recombinant Plasmodium PKG remained active when this residue was mutated. Conformational changes due to cGMP binding appear particularly important for PKG activity. Upon SPARK depletion, multiple N-terminal and cyclic nucleotide-binding domain phosphosites of PKG decrease, suggesting phosphorylation may regulate these domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C141 discuss PKG regulation mechanisms. C138 cites prior work showing T-loop phosphorylation may not be essential, creating uncertainty about the functional significance of T838 down-regulation observed here. C140 documents multiple phosphosite changes, but C141's conclusion that "phosphorylation may function in regulation" is speculative without functional validation.

results.result: The cause for reduction of PKA C1 and PKG levels requires further study. Down-regulation was only observed after 8 hours of SPARK depletion, longer than the T. gondii cell cycle, suggesting dilution through cell division. SPARK could also indirectly stabilize kinase abundances by phosphorylating and inhibiting a ubiquitin ligase.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C144 acknowledge mechanistic uncertainty. C143 provides temporal data supporting dilution, but C144 proposes an alternative ubiquitin-mediated mechanism without direct evidence. The authors appropriately identify this as requiring further study (C142), and the proposed mechanisms remain speculative.

results.result: The authors propose SPARK depletion leads to down-regulation of PKA C3 activity separately from protein abundance changes. SPARK and PKA C3 depletion phenocopy each other regarding in vitro differentiation. Candidates for molecular targets responsible for differentiation may reside in overlapping phosphosites between SPARK and PKA C3 depletion phosphoproteomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C160-C162 propose activity-based regulation of PKA C3. C161 is well-supported by differentiation assays (Figure 6A-B). C160 is a reasonable inference given unchanged protein levels (C111-C113) but decreased PKA C3-dependent phosphopeptides upon SPARK depletion (C118). However, C162 is speculative, as overlapping phosphosites could reflect indirect effects or shared substrates rather than direct differentiation targets.

results.result: The regulation of SPARK remains unclear. Mammalian PDK1 is constitutively active through auto-phosphorylation and PH domain-mediated homodimerization upon PIP3 binding. SPARK lacks the PH domain, suggesting apicomplexans evolved alternative regulatory mechanisms. The SPARK-SPARKEL-TGGT1_205550 complex may represent a means of modulating SPARK activity, but further biochemical studies are required.
results.evaluation: Claims C163-C168, C174 discuss SPARK regulation mechanisms. The absence of the PH domain (C166) is established, and the inference about alternative mechanisms (C167) is reasonable. However, C168's proposal that the SPARKEL complex modulates SPARK activity is speculative. C174 appropriately acknowledges the need for further biochemical studies, as co-depletion complicates interpretation.

results.result: SPARK and SPARKEL IPs and proximity experiments failed to identify obvious components of stable ubiquitin ligase complexes. Unlike most apicomplexans, Plasmodium spp. appear to have lost SPARKEL, possibly requiring alternative mechanisms to control SPARK activity.
results.evaluation: Claim C173 is supported by the IP-MS and TurboID data (Supplementary files 1-3) showing no enrichment of canonical E3 ligase complex components. Claims C175-C176 are supported by phylogenetic analysis (Figure 1C) showing SPARKEL absence in Plasmodium. However, C176's speculation about "alternative mechanisms" is not directly tested.

results.result: SPARK is an apicomplexan ortholog of metazoan PDK1, identified as a fitness-conferring candidate in pooled screens of the T. gondii kinome. PDK1 is considered a key regulator of AGC kinases in mammals. SPARK was previously identified in a genetic screen distinguishing acute and delayed death phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C121, C128 provide background context from prior work (Smith et al., 2022) and established knowledge. The orthology relationship (C1, C121) is well-established in the literature. These claims appropriately cite prior work and are not primary findings of this study.

results.result: Background on apicomplexan biology and second messenger signaling: Apicomplexans parasitize a majority of warm-blooded species. T. gondii acute infection induces disease pathology through invasion, replication, and lysis cycles. Apicomplexans possess complete second messenger signaling repertoires. PKG is necessary for secretion of adhesins and perforins. PKA regulates egress and invasion differently in T. gondii vs. Plasmodium. PKA C3 maintains acute-stage infection. Second messenger networks show documented crosstalk. Metazoan mTOR and PDK1 prime AGC kinases.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C21 provide established background knowledge with appropriate citations. These are not primary findings of this study but contextualize the work. The claims accurately represent prior literature and are well-supported by the cited references.

results.result: Background on AGC kinase regulation: AGC kinases share structural features (activation segment, C-terminal motifs) required for activity. In mammals, AGC kinases depend on PDK1 in various ways. Akt requires PDK1 and mTOR phosphorylation for full activation. PKC isoforms undergo sequential phosphorylation by PDK1. PKA T-loop phosphorylation can be autocatalytic or PDK1-dependent depending on context. PDK1 dysregulation is associated with cancer.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C127 provide background on mammalian AGC kinase regulation with appropriate citations. These establish the conceptual framework for understanding SPARK function but are not primary findings. The claims accurately represent established knowledge in the field.

results.result: Background on PKA and PKG function in apicomplexans: In T. gondii, PKA negatively regulates egress and positively regulates invasion-to-replication transition. In P. falciparum, PKA mediates invasion. PKG is broadly required for motility, invasion, and egress through calcium mobilization. Genetic pathway analysis suggests PKG lies downstream of PKA in T. gondii. Studies implicate negative feedback between cAMP and cGMP pathways. In Plasmodium, PKA is indispensable for invasion but not egress.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C150, C152-C153 provide background on AGC kinase functions in apicomplexans with appropriate citations. These contextualize the current findings but are not primary results. The claims accurately represent prior literature and highlight species-specific differences in signaling.

results.result: Background on PKA C3: T. gondii has two additional PKA catalytic subunit paralogs (PKA C2 and PKA C3) relative to Plasmodium. PKA C2 expression is low outside sexual stages. PKA C3 disruption increases bradyzoite conversion. PKA C3 and SPARK associate through reciprocal interaction approaches.
results.evaluation: Claims C154-C156 provide background with appropriate citations. C157 is a primary finding supported by IP-MS and TurboID data (Figures 3I, 7A). The association between PKA C3 and SPARK is well-documented through multiple approaches.

results.result: Background on Elongin C: Elongin C forms components of multiprotein complexes, with E3 ubiquitin ligases being well-known examples. However, elongin C can affect protein levels through mechanisms distinct from ubiquitination. In metazoans, PDK1 associates with E3 ligases and exhibits monoubiquitination.
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C172 provide background on Elongin C function with appropriate citations. These contextualize the SPARKEL findings but are not primary results. The claims accurately represent established knowledge about Elongin C and PDK1 regulation.

results.result: Summary statements: Unbiased proteomic approaches uncovered ancient signaling network features and revealed repurposing for parasitism. Apicomplexans are well-adapted to transition between life stages. In principle, SPARK may serve as a central node for asexual stage regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C177-C178, C182 are summary/concluding statements. C177 is supported by the comprehensive proteomic analyses presented. C178 is established background. C182 is appropriately qualified as speculative ("in principle, may") and represents a reasonable hypothesis based on the data, though direct evidence for centrality is limited.

results.result: Prior work on SPARK: Parasites depleted of SPARK for multiple replication cycles failed to enter and exit host cells upon zaprinast stimulation. Zaprinast elevates cGMP in parasites. The P. falciparum SPARK ortholog regulates invasion and proliferation through PKA. Parasites with conditional SPARK alleles were previously assessed only after entire lytic cycles. PDK1 mutations in P. falciparum suppress PfPKA overexpression toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5, C22-C23, C129, C133 cite prior work (Smith et al., 2022; Hitz et al., 2021) to provide context. These are not primary findings of this study but establish the rationale for the current investigation. The claims accurately represent the cited literature.

results.result: Background on other proteins: The AGC kinase TGGT1_205550 is restricted to coccidians and dispensable during acute infection. TGGT1_291010 contributes to parasite fitness. Elongin C-like domain function has not been widely investigated in unicellular eukaryotes. PKA C3 is a coccidian-specific PKA ortholog.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C30, C37, C84 provide background information with appropriate citations or inferences from the data. C30 is inferred from the decision to focus on TGGT1_291010 (SPARKEL) rather than TGGT1_205550. These claims appropriately contextualize the study.

results.result: Technical observations: TGGT1_291010 (SPARKEL) is a 23 kDa protein with a C-terminal SKP1/BTB/POZ domain. The low expression level of SPARKEL precluded robust colocalization with SPARK by microscopy.
results.evaluation: Claims C31 and C45 describe technical observations. C31 is supported by sequence analysis and Figure 1B. C45 appropriately acknowledges a technical limitation of the colocalization experiment (Figure 1F), demonstrating appropriate scientific rigor in reporting limitations.

results.result: SPARK physically interacts with an elongin-like protein named SPARKEL (TGGT1_291010), which has a C-terminal SKP1/BTB/POZ domain sharing homology with metazoan Elongin C. This interaction was demonstrated through multiple approaches including immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry and proximity labeling (TurboID), showing consistent enrichment of SPARK and SPARKEL together along with a putative AGC kinase (TGGT1_205550). SPARKEL homologs are found in free-living alveolates but are absent in Aconoidasida, suggesting selective loss in some lineages.
results.evaluation: All three reviewers explicitly praised the study's demonstration of the SPARK-SPARKEL interaction. Reviewer 1 stated the work provides 'compelling evidence for the proposed signalling pathway,' Reviewer 2 called it 'elegantly performed' with 'state-of-the-art proteomic methodologies,' and Reviewer 3 noted 'the data are overall very convincing.' The use of multiple orthogonal approaches (IP-MS, TurboID, reciprocal IPs) to demonstrate the interaction was highlighted as a strength.

results.result: Depletion of SPARKEL using the auxin-inducible degron (AID) system phenocopies SPARK depletion, with both showing reduced invasion and egress efficiency, decreased calcium mobilization, and failed plaque formation after 24 hours of IAA treatment. Importantly, these phenotypes develop over time, with 3 hours of depletion being insufficient to impact motility or calcium signaling, while 24 hours of treatment produces clear defects. The AID system leads to reciprocal co-depletion of SPARK and SPARKEL within 1 hour of IAA treatment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers unanimously accepted these phenotypic findings. Reviewer 2 specifically noted that 'observations from the proteomic datasets are masterfully backed up with validation using quantitative molecular and cellular biology assays.' Reviewer 3 stated 'the work clearly demonstrates that SPARK/SPARKEL regulate invasion and egress.' The time-course experiments showing delayed phenotype development were not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: Extended SPARK or SPARKEL depletion (24 hours) leads to down-regulation of PKG and both catalytic and regulatory subunits of PKA at the protein level, with these changes beginning after 8 hours of IAA treatment. Concomitantly, bradyzoite-specific proteins (MAG1, BRP1, CST1, CST10, MIC13, BFD2) are up-regulated, with increases primarily occurring between 8 and 24 hours of treatment. These kinase subunits were the most down-regulated proteins globally following depletion of either SPARK or SPARKEL.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly endorsed these proteomic findings. Reviewer 2 described the work as using 'quantitative (phospho)proteomic techniques to elegantly demonstrate the upstream role of SPARK in controlling cAMP and cGMP pathways' and praised the 'sophisticated analysis techniques.' Reviewer 1 noted the use of 'advanced proteomic and functional approaches provides compelling evidence.' No concerns were raised about the proteomics data quality or interpretation.

results.result: Phosphoproteomic analysis of SPARK depletion identified 18,518 phosphopeptides, revealing broad effects on post-translational modification cascades. SPARK depletion reduced phosphopeptide abundance of cyclic nucleotide-regulated kinases and several phosphatases (BCC6, PPM1), while affecting proteins involved in DNA accessibility, transcription, RNA modification, and metabolic transport. Gaussian mixture-model clustering identified seven distinct response classes, implicating SPARK in numerous cellular processes including signaling, gene regulation, and metabolic exchange.
results.evaluation: Reviewers praised the phosphoproteomic approach without raising concerns about data quality or interpretation. Reviewer 2 specifically highlighted the 'sophisticated analysis techniques' and stated the work 'set a new benchmark for the use of proteomics and molecular genetics in apicomplexan parasites.' Reviewer 3 noted the study is 'very well executed with appropriate controls.' The only concern raised was by Reviewer 3 about 'incomplete data analysis,' but this was noted as improved in the revised manuscript.

results.result: Proximity labeling experiments using SPARK-TurboID showed enrichment of PKG and PKA C3, with PKA C1 narrowly missing cutoffs. A putative HECT E3 ubiquitin ligase with down-regulated phosphosites was also identified as a candidate interactor. These experiments suggest that SPARK, PKA, and PKG are spatially associated within the parasite cell.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the proximity labeling data as supporting evidence for SPARK's role in regulating AGC kinases. Reviewer 2 noted the authors 'use sophisticated analysis techniques to show the functional association between cGMP and cAMP signalling pathways.' The integration of proximity labeling with other approaches was viewed as a strength, with no concerns raised about the TurboID methodology or interpretation.

results.result: SPARK depletion reduces specific phosphorylation sites on PKA C1 (T190 in activation loop, T341 in C-terminal tail) and PKA R (S17, S27, S94 in N-terminus), with protein abundance decreasing predominantly after 8 hours of IAA treatment as measured by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry. Transcript levels remain unchanged, indicating post-transcriptional regulation. PKA C1-dependent phosphopeptides significantly decreased in abundance between 8 and 24 hours of SPARK depletion compared to the bulk phosphoproteome.
results.evaluation: Reviewers endorsed these findings as part of the comprehensive characterization of SPARK's effects on PKA. Reviewer 2 stated that 'observations from the proteomic datasets are masterfully backed up with validation using quantitative molecular and cellular biology assays.' The multi-level validation (phosphoproteomics, immunofluorescence, flow cytometry, qRT-PCR) was viewed positively, with no concerns raised about the conclusions.

results.result: SPARK depletion reduces phosphorylation of PKG at multiple N-terminal sites and the activation loop (T838). Functionally, SPARK depletion sensitizes parasites to the PKG inhibitor Compound 1 in A23187-induced egress assays, suggesting decreased PKG activity. PKG-dependent phosphopeptides significantly decreased in abundance between 8 and 24 hours of SPARK depletion compared to the bulk phosphoproteome.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as demonstrating SPARK's regulation of PKG. Reviewer 2 noted the authors 'elegantly demonstrate the upstream role of SPARK in controlling cAMP and cGMP pathways.' The functional validation using PKG inhibitor sensitization was not questioned, and the integration of phosphoproteomics with functional assays was praised.

results.result: Prolonged SPARK, SPARKEL, or PKA C3 depletion elevates differentiation to bradyzoites under both normal and alkaline stress conditions, as measured by cyst wall staining with dolichos binding lectin. This differentiation phenotype is similar across all three depletions and depends on the BFD1 transcriptional circuit, as SPARK- and PKA C3-AID/Δbfd1 mutants fail to undergo differentiation. The differentiation proceeds through the canonical transcriptional pathway, with up-regulation of chronic-stage proteins including BAG1, CST1, CST10, MIC13, and TgSPT2.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly endorsed these differentiation findings. Reviewer 1 noted the study 'identifies protein kinases...that are required for...differentiation to drug-resistant chronic stages.' Reviewer 2 stated the authors 'extend their work by showing that SPARK/SPARKEL also control PKAc3 function' and that 'PKAc3 has previously been shown to negatively regulate differentiation into bradyzoite forms and this work backs up and extends this finding.' The genetic validation using the Δbfd1 mutant was not questioned.

results.result: PKA C3 physically interacts with SPARK, as demonstrated by reciprocal immunoprecipitation-mass spectrometry showing high enrichment of SPARK in PKA C3 IPs and significant co-purification of SPARKEL. This is consistent with TurboID proximity labeling data and with prior reports that PKA C3 does not interact with the canonical PKA regulatory subunit in T. gondii, supporting a strong physical interaction between SPARK and PKA C3.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the PKA C3-SPARK interaction data. Reviewer 2 noted the authors 'extend their work by showing that SPARK/SPARKEL also control PKAc3 function' and praised the use of 'molecular and cellular assays on a range of generated transgenic lines to back up their observations.' The reciprocal IP approach and consistency with prior literature were not questioned.

results.result: Unlike PKA C1 and PKG, PKA C3 protein levels do not decrease following SPARK depletion. After 24 hours of IAA treatment, PKA C3 levels were unaltered or slightly elevated by immunoblot, with immunofluorescence and flow cytometry showing a non-significant trend toward increasing abundance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this differential regulation of PKA C3 compared to other AGC kinases. Reviewer 2 noted the careful characterization showing that 'SPARK also controls' PKA C3, and the distinction between protein abundance and activity was not challenged. The data were viewed as part of the comprehensive characterization of SPARK's effects on different AGC kinases.

results.result: PKA C3 depletion phosphoproteomics identified 4,792 proteins and 12,721 phosphopeptides, with PCA separating 24-hour IAA samples from controls. Several up-regulated proteins were bradyzoite stage markers (BRP1, TGGT1_208740, BFD2). PKA C3-dependent phosphopeptides significantly decreased within 3 hours of SPARK depletion (faster than PKA C1 or PKG effects). The SPARK and PKA C3 phosphoproteomes share signatures of reduced PKA C3 activity but diverge regarding dense granule protein regulation, with some PKA C3-dependent phosphopeptides increasing upon SPARK depletion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers endorsed the PKA C3 phosphoproteomics as part of the comprehensive analysis. Reviewer 2 praised the 'sophisticated analysis techniques' and noted the work 'set a new benchmark for the use of proteomics.' The comparative analysis between SPARK and PKA C3 depletion phosphoproteomes was not questioned, and the divergence in dense granule protein regulation was accepted as presented.

results.result: The authors propose a model in which SPARK is required for the activation and stabilization of PKG, PKA C1, and PKA C3. Genetic evidence supports that SPARK phenotypes associated with lytic cycle transitions (motility, egress, invasion) arise from dysregulated PKA C1 and PKG activities. In T. gondii, SPARK inhibition releases the brakes that PKA C1 holds on egress while reducing PKG activity, resulting in parasite stasis. SPARK fundamentally integrates cyclic nucleotide signaling networks, with proper SPARK function preserving tachyzoite physiology and promoting acute stage cycling over differentiation to bradyzoites.
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly endorsed the proposed model and its implications. Reviewer 2 stated the authors 'begin to unify our understanding of the complicated signalling pathways used by Toxoplasma' and noted 'the paper is carefully and concisely written and is not overreaching in its conclusions.' Reviewer 1 described it as a 'fundamental study' with 'compelling evidence for the proposed signalling pathway.' Reviewer 3 stated 'the work clearly demonstrates that SPARK/SPARKEL regulate invasion and egress and that their loss triggers differentiation.'

results.result: Sequence analysis reveals that TgPKG and TgPKA C1 possess features of AGC kinases involved in PDK1 interaction, including PDK1-interacting fragment (PIF) motifs: PKA C1 terminates in FTSW, PKG has two non-terminal FXXF motifs (FGDF and FLYF), and PKA C3 possesses a canonical PIF (FDNF) and shares an activation loop motif with PKA C1. The T-loop phosphorylation sites of PKA C1 (T190) and PKG (T838) were detected in the phosphoproteome and down-regulated following SPARK knockdown.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the sequence analysis and its implications for SPARK-AGC kinase interactions. Reviewer 2 noted the work demonstrates 'the upstream role of SPARK in controlling cAMP and cGMP pathways' and that the authors 'use sophisticated analysis techniques.' The structural features supporting PDK1-like interactions were not questioned and were viewed as supporting the proposed regulatory mechanism.

results.result: Phylogenetic analysis shows SPARKEL homologs are found in free-living alveolates (Vitrella brassicaformis and Chromera velia) but are absent in Aconoidasida, suggesting the gene was present in the ancestor of apicomplexans but selectively lost in some lineages. Unlike most apicomplexans, Plasmodium spp. appear to have lost SPARKEL, possibly requiring alternative mechanisms to control SPARK activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the phylogenetic analysis without raising concerns. Reviewer 1 noted the work 'will be of broad interest to cell biologists and parasitologists,' implicitly accepting the evolutionary context. The speculation about alternative mechanisms in Plasmodium was appropriately framed as a hypothesis and not challenged by reviewers.

results.result: Upon SPARK depletion, multiple phosphorylation sites in the N-terminal and cyclic nucleotide-binding domains of PKG (T16, S20, S22, T59, S62, T96, T99, S129) decrease in abundance, while others remain stable or increase (S40, S105). This suggests phosphorylation may function in the regulation of these domains.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these detailed phosphorylation site analyses as part of the comprehensive phosphoproteomic characterization. Reviewer 2 praised the 'state-of-the-art proteomic methodologies' and noted observations were 'masterfully backed up with validation.' The interpretation that phosphorylation regulates these domains was not questioned.

results.result: The complex of proteins interacting with SPARK—the elongin-like protein SPARKEL and the putative AGC kinase TGME49_205550—may represent a means of modulating SPARK activity. However, further biochemical studies are required to discern the regulatory interactions between SPARK and SPARKEL, particularly given the co-depletion observed with the AID system.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accepted the identification of the SPARK-SPARKEL complex, the mechanistic understanding of how this complex regulates SPARK activity remains unclear. Reviewer 3 noted that 'the primary concern of incomplete data analysis still needs to be addressed' in the revised manuscript, suggesting some aspects of the mechanism require further investigation. The authors themselves acknowledge this limitation, stating 'further biochemical studies are required.'
